title: Mapping Two Schemas to a Canonical Schema
description: Match differently-named fields from two source systems to a canonical schema and read each transformation rule.
creator: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
Knowledge Representation and Metadata

educational.learningObjective: Given two source schemas with differently-named fields, the learner will identify which fields correspond to the same canonical concept and state the transformation rule that maps one to the other.
prerequisites: Knows what a database field is
Has seen two systems that store overlapping data
learningOutcomes: Identify which source fields correspond to the same canonical concept
State the transformation rule for a given mapping
Explain why matching is a judgment about meaning rather than about spelling
educational.assessmentOpportunity: Give learners a third source system with fields like customer_full_name and contact_email, and ask for the two mapping rules including any needed transformation.

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Click-node-or-edge inspection with a summary mode
pedagogical.instructionalStrategy: Separating two easily-conflated concepts by giving each its own clickable element
pedagogical.feedbackType: Distinct explanations for matching (nodes) and mapping (edges)
misconceptionsAddressed: That schema matching and schema mapping are the same step
That matched fields always need a direct copy
discussionQuestions: Who decides what the canonical definition of 'customer' is?
What is lost when two fields are declared equivalent and they are not quite?
Why does the hub pattern from Chapter 18 reappear here?
